articles.body:
Nigeria: Upcoming elections marred by rising AI disinformation

November 14, 2026

As Nigeria inches closer to the 2027 polls, the use of artificial intelligence in the electoral process has prompted questions about integrity and institutional readiness. Can Nigerians trust their democratic processes?

Nigeria has just over two months to go to the polls, with incumbent President Bola Tinubu running on a ticket focused on combating raging insecurity and resolving the nation's economic crisis. He faces off against former Vice President Atiku Abubakar and senior opposition figure Peter Obi.

The country's electoral body, the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), recently released its preliminary voter's register, which reportedly is riddled with images believed to have been generated using artificial intelligence (AI).

Among the telltale signs of AI usage were exaggerated facial features in images, and inconsistencies on the electoral registers, such as duplicates of names and even identities of people who since the previous election had died.

The development raises concerns about the body's overall preparedness ahead of the country's upcoming 2027 general elections; instead of making the upcoming vote more transparent by allowing access to its procedures, INEC has come under fire amid broader controversies about the expanding influence of AI in elections across the continent.

Fake news: Nothing new in Nigeria

Joash Amupitan, the chairman of the commission, said the body is now investigating the development, focusing on discrepancies potentially created by AI-use.

To this end, he announced the establishment of a dedicated unit to monitor AI-related threats, detect deepfakes and strengthen the integrity of the electoral process, warning that the credibility of the upcoming elections could otherwise be under attack.

However, even prior to the proliferation of AI across Africa and indeed the globe, this would not be the first time that Nigeria finds itself in the unfortunate position of having to deal with the circulation of fabricated images, doctored audio and fake videos online; in the run up to the 2023 elections, deepfakes falsely linking candidates to terror-related activities filled social media platforms.

These are often designed to promote certain candidates, or to discredit opponents in a bid to influence public perception, which now with the use of AI could create disinformation campaigns of new proportions.

Artificial Intelligence: Various effects on voter behavior

Lois Ugbede, the assistant editor at the factchecking platform DUBAWA, told DW that "based on our monitoring so far, AI-driven disinformation is serious and is becoming commonplace."

"This could influence political discourse and voter behavior ahead of 2027 because we are already seeing parties using inflated crowds to show that they have a large followership or support," she added.

At the same time, rather than influencing the vote in favor of any particular candidate, "the deeper danger is that people may begin to doubt authentic information simply because they know convincing AI generated fakes are possible," says Akintunde Babatunde, Executive Director of the Abuja-based Center for Journalism, Innovation and Development (CJID)."

"We often focus on the risk of people believing an AI-generated falsehood, but there is another problem where genuine evidence can be dismissed as AI generated," he noted, citing instances of a lawmaker who recently made inflammatory remarks during a campaign rally — but then claimed the clips were manipulated.

Further pitfalls behind a lack of safeguards against AI

Chibuike Mgbeahuruike, an election consultant at the Centre for Democracy and Development (CDD-West Africa), meanwhile told DW that apart from the spread of synthetic content online, AI intrusion into INEC's portal could also "undermine its institutional credibility, especially with the low level of confidence that we are already witnessing."

He added however that AI itself is not inherently a threat to electoral integrity, but that the real threat rather lies in "the absence of effective accountability for its deployment," as innovations in tech increasingly appear to infiltrate governments and their democratic processes.

"Voters must have confidence … that the technology is also transparent, accountable and independently scrutinized, and ultimately subject to human and institutional oversight," Mgbeahuruike said.

The Director-General of Voice of Nigeria (VON), Mallam Jibrin Baba Ndace, agrees, urging journalists at a recent conference also to not fall into the trap of believing reports, which later could turn out to be false due to AI manipulation.

He stressed the importance of protection measures and due diligence in news media, with the growing inability of public institutions like INEC to provide impartial information due to the use and influence of AI and other election-related tech.

Nigeria's marred relationship with new tech in elections

Beyond AI, Nigeria's electoral processes have undergone various technological shifts over the years in hopes of improving transparency while increasing efficiency.

Electoral authorities first deployed electronic assistance in 2011, when Direct Data Capture Machines were introduced; the devices collect voters' biometrics by scanning fingerprints or capturing facial recognition data with webcams to stop voters from submitting multiple ballots.

Ten years later, a new system called the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS) was introduced as the new standard, designed to combine fingerprints with facial recognition; however, during the 2023 general elections, this voting process was marred by system failures of BVAS, as poor cell signal delayed these voter accreditation procedures.

However, with INEC tallying more than 103 million Nigerians registered to participate in the coming poll, disinformation, fake news and technological challenges amount to only few of several concerns pertaining to Nigeria's democracy:

Voter apathy has become a particular concern, especially among the country's youth; the 2023 elections recorded the lowest voter turnout since the country's return to democratic rule in 1999, with merely 27 percent of registered voters going to the polls.

articles.title: Jensen Huang’s departure blasts big hole in AI startup funding, VCs and founders say
articles.summary: Nvidia poured tens of billions into AI startups under Huang. Without him at the helm, founders and VCs are bracing for smaller checks and lower valuations.
articles.preview: It was the resignation heard across the world. Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s embattled CEO who co-founded and led the company for 33 years, had officially stepped down. “It’s like a bomb went off,” one neocloud founder told TechCrunch when he first heard the news. Over the last several years, Nvidia has been a prolific investor, pouring tens of billions into startups annually and participating in 105 rounds this year alone, often as the largest investor, according to PitchBook.
articles.body:
It was the resignation heard across the world. Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s embattled CEO who co-founded and led the company for 33 years, had officially stepped down. “It’s like a bomb went off,” one neocloud founder told TechCrunch when he first heard the news.

Over the last several years, Nvidia has been a prolific investor, pouring tens of billions into startups annually and participating in 105 rounds this year alone, often as the largest investor, according to PitchBook. “If that direction changes, it’ll be a big blow to so many young companies,” said Maria Davidson, founder of Relational Capital.

Huang’s absence leaves the startup ecosystem without one of its biggest champions and with far less capital for now, investors say, which could have a massive impact on dealmaking, valuations, funding, and even competition.

“Nvidia is carrying almost every AI-native startup from application to neocloud,” Dawn Capital’s Shamillah Bankiya told TechCrunch.

Most of the significant decisions to invest in startups often came from Jensen himself, according to Umesh Padval, managing partner at Seligman Ventures. Padval has known Huang since serving on the board of Mellanox Technologies, a networking chipmaker Nvidia acquired for approximately $7 billion in 2020. While there is hope that Huang’s eventual successor will resume his dealmaking spree, investors aren’t hopeful that it will happen in the short term.

Nvidia’s interim CEO, Colette Kress, is expected to institute some changes, especially when it comes to Nvidia’s investments into AI startups at the crux of the billion-dollar data center build-out. Huang’s rampant dealmaking in this sphere has been a source of concern for Wall Street.

“She’s much more conservative,” one investor said of Kress. “I don’t think she’s going to commit the same amount of money to keep the early-stage ecosystem going.”

Nvidia’s biggest bets were backing neoclouds, inference providers, and open weight models, which are expensive for smaller companies to build. “Jensen’s initiatives are a big reason an ecosystem has emerged despite that,” Zain Javaid, co-founder of the hardware company Ghost, said.

For instance, Nvidia backed CoreWeave when it was still private and participated in two of Crusoe’s rounds, including its $1.4 billion Series E. It bought Hugging Face this year for $13 billion (expected to close in 2027) and holds investments in Mistral AI, Lambda, and Black Forest Labs. Nvidia was often the largest investor in the deals. Last year, it wrote an $800 million check into a $2 billion Series B round for Reflection AI, before the open source startup began to earn meaningful revenue, according to the Wall Street Journal.

“Jensen believed in open source and frankly speaking, Europe,” Bankiya said of how Huang invested so much in AI across the world. The cease of that support in other regions outside of America, like Europe “would be a massive funding and honestly ecosystem gap that no one can fill.”

It’s also true that Nvidia was such a dominant player in the ecosystem that at times, it felt like a monopoly. By backing so many companies with such generous checks, Nvidia effectively locked those startups into using its chips, which helped reinforce its dominant market position.

If the company does grow more conservative with its startup investments, that could leave more room for rivals and smaller competitors. (Coincidentally, Google announced two new chips this week amid Huang’s Nvidia fallout.)

Some investors with whom TechCrunch spoke hope that large cloud companies and other chipmakers will step in to back startups and fill some of the void that will likely be left by Huang.

Dharmesh Thakker, a general partner at Battery Ventures, for example, expects Big Tech rivals to vie for Nvidia’s investment crown, “depending upon who brings the best combination of a great product, an ecosystem and community to compete with CUDA, and the financial power to bankroll the ecosystem,” he said. CUDA is Nvidia’s software platform that enables developers to run AI models on its GPUs.

While companies like Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and AMD may back mature startups to drive adoption of their chips and clouds, Thakker doubts they will pour hundreds of millions into pre-revenue infrastructure startups the way Nvidia did.

Under Huang, infrastructure companies that needed $100 million to $500 million in GPUs would often raise half of that amount at valuations of $1 billion or more from Nvidia just to get started, one VC said. The chipmaker’s participation gave other investors the comfort in backing these companies at the lofty valuations.

Now Nvidia is expected to be more selective in the new companies it backs, while writing smaller-sized checks into its existing portfolio, contributing to a drop in valuations.

“When Nvidia was on the cap table, everyone felt safe,” Padval said. Without that backing, investors say traditional VCs are likely to think twice before writing checks into these startups and may even pause certain dealmaking.

Even so, few believe that Nvidia’s investment slowdown will by itself halt the broader AI boom.

Though everyone agrees that Huang is a massive loss for Nvidia, one of his ex-employees, Amulya Vishwanath, who now runs her own VC fund, said that “founders and leaders must be held accountable,” and that the ecosystem is bigger than one person. “That talent will, and must, continue to thrive.”

articles.body:
After launching its Dots AI agents platform earlier this year, OpenAI is launching a wallet for the agents. ChatGPT Wallet is rolling out starting today for ChatGPT Pro subscribers in the US aged 18 and older using a US billing address and “eligible US-issued American Express, Chase, Mastercard and Visa cards.”

OpenAI says ChatGPT Wallet won’t share your actual credit card info with its AI agents.

After adding a card to the wallet, your Dots agents can use it to buy things in response to your prompts, but they’ll check in with you each time before checking out. OpenAI’s support page says every purchase with ChatGPT Wallet requires a security check with biometric verification like Face ID or a fingerprint scan.

After you review the AI agent’s purchase and sign off on it, OpenAI says that, similar to using tap to pay, Apple Pay, or Google Wallet, it substitutes your credit card details with a payment token, so your actual card info isn’t shared with your Dots agent or the business you’re buying from. Eventually, OpenAI says it expects “users to be able to delegate purchases entirely to their agent by setting clear parameters—such as spending limits, purchase categories, or time periods—and pre-approve those purchases.”

ChatGPT Wallet might not work everywhere. Some retailers have restrictions on AI agents or block them altogether. Earlier this year, Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse agents. OpenAI says that in order for agents to use ChatGPT Wallet, “websites need to ensure agents are not inadvertently blocked, and payment and risk systems need to recognize legitimate purchases made by agents.”

articles.body:
Anyone who has weathered a hurricane can tell you that the oceans — which fuel the storms — contain a tremendous amount of energy. Thanks to global warming, they’re holding more than ever.

A new startup wants to harness that energy to power data centers.

Drogue, which has kept a low profile until now, is building a system that harvests heat from the ocean to power data centers on board floating vessels. According to founder and CEO Sam Sipe, the first prototype should be bobbing around the ocean, crunching bits, less than two years from now.

The goal, Sipe said, is to help data center developers deploy servers in AI-friendly timelines. “The data center industry is a real estate game, and so they’re playing on 8- to 10-year timelines, including interoperability with utilities and [independent system operators]” that manage regional power grids, he said. “AI demand has increased 10x in just the last three years. It’s completely incompatible.”

Drogue was founded just six months ago in Washington, D.C., and the startup told TechCrunch exclusively that it has already raised $20 million, including from XYZ Venture Capital, Toyota Ventures, Tamarack Global, Dream, FDVC, Garuda Ventures, Flexcap, Boost VC, and Slow Ventures, among other investors.

In those six months, Drogue has designed a multi-megawatt prototype that will be installed on a traditional oceangoing ship and sent out to sea in early 2028. Future versions will be built on floating structures that more closely resemble offshore oil platforms.

To Sipe, the decision to turn to the ocean was obvious.

After years flying E-2D Hawkeyes off U.S. Navy aircraft carriers, he had an appreciation for the ocean’s immense power. “Most people think, oh, ocean — hard waves, storms, corrosion, biofouling. And I just see this majestic place and resource that we just ignore,” he said.

As the planet warms, the oceans have been absorbing an additional 5.8 million terawatt-hours of energy every year. By comparison, all of human civilization uses about 180,000 terawatt-hours each year. If Drogue were to take some, surely the ocean wouldn’t miss it.

The startup’s technology works like a heat pump run in reverse. A heat pump uses electricity to move heat from one place to another; Drogue’s system instead uses a difference in temperature to generate electricity. This approach, known as ocean thermal energy conversion, or OTEC, was first developed in the 1950s.

Surface waters are warmer, heated by the sun, while down-deep temperatures are much colder, about 39°F on average (4°C). “There’s basically no amount of heat we can pull out of that that will collapse that temperature differential,” Sipe said.

To leverage the temperature differential, the startup’s system draws in warm surface water, uses it to cool the data centers, and then sends the now-warmer water to boil ammonia, a chemical that turns to gas at -28°F. That ammonia gas is then sent through a turbine to generate electricity. Once through the turbine, it courses through a condenser, which turns the gas back into a liquid. There, cold water drawn from 1,000 meters deep passes over the condenser’s fins to absorb the heat. The warmed water is then released, and dissipates into the ocean. The ammonia gets sent back to the start of the sealed loop, and the cycle repeats.

The basic idea was tested in the 1980s but tossed aside. “A lot has changed since the ’80s, specifically manufacturing techniques around the pipe and the heat exchangers,” Sipe said.

To find out why, Sipe sought out people who had worked on those early efforts. “I just talked to everyone, basically interviewed them and figured out what went wrong, what went right, what would you do next. And everyone was like, dude, this stuff works. It’s just a matter of being able to raise enough capital to build something big enough, because there’s a sweet spot,” he said.

There also had to be customers who could use that power while still at sea. Sending power to shore would require lengthy, expensive cables, and manufacturing on board would require similarly expensive shipping of materials and finished goods. Data centers are ideal — the servers are compact relative to other equipment, and shipping data off the platform is incredibly cheap. Each vessel would live at sea for about a decade, Sipe said.

Drogue already has “approval in principle,” a preliminary sign-off, from the American Bureau of Shipping, which sets and checks safety standards for ships. Now it’s in the process of buying its first ship to start building a prototype ready for the open ocean.

In many ways, Drogue’s concept is similar to Elon Musk’s plan for orbital data centers: find a cheap source of power, and get the data centers as close to it as possible. Except unlike orbital data centers, Drogue’s don’t need to launch expensive rockets to get there. They can just sail a ship on the ocean, something humanity has been doing for millennia.

articles.body:
Agent management startup LangChain has raised a $300 million Series C at a $3 billion valuation led by CapitalG, with participation from investors, including Singapore’s GIC, DFJ Growth, IVP, and Sapphire Ventures, the company announced on Friday.

That’s more than double its $1.25 billion valuation when it raised $125 million about a year ago, led by IVP.

LangChain began in 2022 as a popular open source project that handled the kinds of tasks that early-stage LLMs found difficult, like searching the web, calling APIs, and interacting with databases. As the frontier AI labs delivered harnesses that now competently do those tasks, LangChain turned its focus toward managing AI agents. It has apparently found its stride in this highly competitive area with a simple message: letting businesses own their own intelligence.

With its open source roots, the startup says its agent creation and management software, LangSmith, is not trying to lock users into any particular model, cloud, or ecosystem, unlike the major clouds or frontier AI labs. It also promises that LangSmith will contain agent behavior and is easy to use.

True, there are plenty of other startups pitching similar advantages these days and also doing well (case in point is newcomer Mintive). However, LangChain has had a head start and now claims 7,000 LangSmith customers, including big-name startups like Harvey, Rippling, and Clay, and enterprises like Nvidia, Toyota, and Salesforce.

articles.body:
Under cofounder Jensen Huang, Nvidia has become the engine for the AI boom — and one of the tech industry’s biggest environmental liabilities. Its sought-after chips have triggered a new wave of water- and chemical-intensive factories, drained power grids from inside massive data centers, and set the stage for a looming e-waste problem.

Nvidia’s environmental footprint extends way beyond its own offices.

Under Huang’s leadership, Nvidia clashed with environmental groups seeking to hold the company accountable for its so-called “hidden” emissions. Huang has talked up the idea of using AI to fight climate change while his company’s supply chain emissions ballooned. Nvidia’s investments, meanwhile, have supported the buildout of data centers that have sparked intense backlash for both their local and global impact. Now, after the CEO’s shocking resignation amid a sprawling sex-and-espionage scandal, advocates are urging Nvidia to turn the page.

He compared AI to a surgeon who has “to cut you open to save you.”

“Jensen Huang has failed to put climate responsibility at the heart of the company’s growth strategy, to slow down the unchecked expansion of data centres or to prevent its chips from being deployed in unethical applications like automated warfare,” Avex Li, Greenpeace East Asia’s project lead for AI supply chain campaign, said in a press release Thursday. The organization is now pushing interim CEO Colette Kress to commit Nvidia to decarbonizing by investing in renewable energy, as well as ensuring its technology is used in a way that “respects human rights.” Nvidia didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment from The Verge.

Huang has projected optimism about how AI can boost the adoption of renewable energy, even as the planet-heating emissions of tech companies — including his own — have grown in the generative AI era. “If you want to turn a corner on climate change, if you want a future that’s sustainable, lean into A.I. It is the best opportunity we have to get there,” Huang said in a September episode of The Ezra Klein Show, arguing that electricity demand for AI is leading companies to buy more sustainable energy.

In the same interview, however, he admitted data centers will rely on more fossil fuels in the near term, and that building up the infrastructure for AI will likely result in “an enormous amount of pain and suffering.” He compared AI to a surgeon who has “to cut you open to save you.”

Nvidia’s supply-chain emissions have grown 725 percent since 2020, according to an analysis of the company’s public disclosures by research analyst Ketan Joshi and several environmental organizations, including Greenpeace and Climate Action Against Disinformation, published in September. It’s an increase of about 9.4 million metric tons of planet-heating pollution, roughly equivalent to the emissions from nearly 25 gas plants over a year. Supply chain emissions the company disclosed for fiscal year 2026 reached around 10.7 million metric tons of CO2, according to Nvidia’s latest sustainability report.

Joshi and his co-authors approximated how much greenhouse gas pollution comes from the use of chips the company sells, a category Nvidia doesn’t include in its sustainability reports. Those emissions could have reached 21 million metric tons in 2025, according to the report, based on estimated chip power consumption. That level of pollution puts Nvidia on par with Russia’s state-owned coal company, according to Joshi.

Those “indirect” emissions — from its supply chain and the use of its products — make up the bulk of Nvidia’s climate impact. The carbon footprint of facilities Nvidia actually owns and operates looks much smaller in comparison because Nvidia designs chips that other companies like TSMC then manufacture. Greenhouse gas emissions coming directly from Nvidia-operated facilities and vehicles only reached 9,822 metric tons in fiscal year 2026, the company’s sustainability report shows. And in 2025, the company reached a goal of matching 100 percent of its facilities’ electricity use with clean energy purchases.

Greenpeace wants Nvidia to extend that goal to its entire manufacturing supply chain. When Greenpeace activists disrupted Huang’s speech at Nvidia GTC in Berlin last month, he responded onstage by saying, “I’ll talk to you guys later … All important issues, but let me get through my keynote.” In the Thursday press release, Greenpeace says Nvidia has yet to meet with Greenpeace despite the organization’s attempts to “seek dialogue” with the company over the past two years.

“One of Huang’s defining legacies is inflating a speculative AI bubble, pouring billions of dollars into infrastructure with little regard for the real-world consequences inflicted on local communities and the climate,” Katrin Wu, Big Tech campaigner at Greenpeace International, said in an email to The Verge. “Huang may be gone, but the ‘tech colonialism’ Nvidia perpetuates continues.”

“Huang may be gone, but the ‘tech colonialism’ Nvidia perpetuates continues.”

Beyond Nvidia’s day-to-day operations, Huang threw his weight around as the CEO of one of the world’s most valuable companies — chumming it up with President Donald Trump and lobbying for the US to allow sales of its powerful chips to China. The company’s influence on the global economy extended beyond chips as it invested in data centers stocking its GPUs.

And with electricity supply often the thorniest bottleneck to building more and bigger data centers, Nvidia’s long tendrils reached into the energy sector as well. NVentures, the company’s venture capital arm, has funded battery recycling company Redwood Materials and startups developing AI tools to optimize power grids and make data centers more responsive to fluctuations in energy demand.

Nvidia joined one of those startups, Emerald AI, along with Google to cofound the AI Energy Management Alliance (AEMA) in September. The alliance advocates for strategies that tech companies promote as ways to keep data centers from overwhelming power grids or raising utility bills for other customers, including generating power on-site and making “flexible” facilities that can pause operations during times of peak energy demand. Notably, some environmental groups argue that those measures might just help data centers come online faster without fully insulating households from the impact that rising electricity demand has on their air quality or utility bills.

Whether Nvidia’s environmental footprint shrinks or expands from here will depend on whoever steps in to fill Huang’s shoes. Over the years, Greenpeace and other environmental groups have pointed out that despite having an outsize impact on the environment, Nvidia doesn’t necessarily come under the same public scrutiny as more consumer-facing brands like Apple or Google. Huang’s exploits have thrust the company into a new kind of spotlight, however, just as data centers increasingly face backlash from nearby communities. Nvidia won’t be able to hide from the glare.

articles.title: Is the AI bubble bursting just as Anthropic goes public?
articles.summary: The sharp sell-off in tech stocks after the US midterms has cast doubt on Anthropic's looming IPO. Yet with hundreds of billions still being invested, some think the AI party is still in full swing.
articles.preview: November 13, 2026 The sharp sell-off in tech stocks after the US midterms has cast doubt on Anthropic's looming IPO. Yet with hundreds of billions still being invested, some think the AI party is still in full swing. 2026 was meant to be the year Wall Street’s trillion-dollar artificial intelligence (AI) bet started paying off. Instead, it’s turning into a test of nerves. In the first half of the year, many AI stocks hit record highs as US hyperscalers like Google's Alphabet, Meta and Microsoft recorded bumper earnings.
articles.body:
November 13, 2026

The sharp sell-off in tech stocks after the US midterms has cast doubt on Anthropic's looming IPO. Yet with hundreds of billions still being invested, some think the AI party is still in full swing.

2026 was meant to be the year Wall Street’s trillion-dollar artificial intelligence (AI) bet started paying off. Instead, it’s turning into a test of nerves.

In the first half of the year, many AI stocks hit record highs as US hyperscalers like Google's Alphabet, Meta and Microsoft recorded bumper earnings.

Two of the largest AI players — Anthropic and OpenAI — announced plans for public listings, following SpaceX's much-hyped IPO in June, which briefly made Elon Musk the world's first trillionaire.

AI models, meanwhile, got noticeably better at difficult tasks in the race to beat human intelligence.

AI doubts trigger market turbulence

The second half of 2026, however, has brought a lot more uncertainty. While the stock of Nvidia, a chipmaker, pushed even higher last month, many hyperscalers and chip or memory firms have seen their stock prices gyrate wildly.

Then last week, after the Democrats secured control of the United States Congress in the midterm elections, technology stocks sold off dramatically, with the Magnificent Seven — including Meta, Apple, Amazon and Tesla — losing more than $1 trillion in value in a single trading day.

In a further twist, the AI sector took another hit this week as Nvidia shares plunged nearly 10% over two days. The sell-off followed news that Nvidia's board — alongside the FBI — is investigating CEO Jensen Huang’s ties to a woman suspected by US intelligence of being a Chinese spy.

On Thursday, Huang resigned from the chipmaker when a second alleged affair was revealed, sending Nvidia's shares lower still.

Amid huge spending, big returns remain elusive

Wall Street is growing increasingly cautious about the sheer size of the AI outlay, amid warnings that future earnings may not justify the huge spending. Growing pressure on US lawmakers to curb the expansion of AI data centers has added to those doubts.

In September, investment bank Goldman Sachs estimated that hyperscalers need around $300 billion in annual AI revenue to break even on their spending, leaving a gap of roughly $230 billion.

"We're not in Kansas anymore," Dennis Dick, chief market strategist at the Canada-based Stock Trader Network, told DW, meaning that times have changed. Now, he said, investors are telling companies: "Show me the money."

AI stocks needed a 'healthy correction'

Other analysts think it's too soon to expect the AI bubble to burst, including Kit Rees, investment strategist at London-based wealth manager Quilter, who thinks last week's rout was a "healthy correction."

"We’re still in the very early innings of the AI build-out," Rees told DW. "There’s still a lot of excitement around this technology and investors will want to have a slice of the pie."

In addition to the roughly $800 billion invested in capital expenditures this year, AI hyperscalers plan to spend a further $1.2 trillion in 2027 and $1.4 trillion in 2028, according to Goldman Sachs estimates.

Questions over timing of Anthropic IPO

While OpenAI has delayed its public listing until next year, Claude-maker Anthropic still plans its IPO later this month. On Tuesday, the company said it would offer 825 million shares at between $70 and $78 per share.

Dick said Anthropic’s decision to go ahead amid the market sell-off left him scratching his head.

"Is this the best timing?" he asked.

While Anthropic had originally targeted a valuation of over $2 trillion, it now thinks the firm could be worth around $1.2 trillion to $1.3 trillion.

Dick said the valuation depends on whether Anthropic can deliver on a forecast by Goldman Sachs of more than $600 billion in revenue by 2030.

"If you get to a company with $600 billion in revenue, [a] $1.3 trillion [valuation] doesn’t sound that bad," he told DW. "But when you’re talking about a company with currently $52 billion in revenue, it sounds like it’s overvalued."

Other analysts, like Vivek Seth, chief executive officer of Shaires Holdings, are more bullish about the Claude-maker's prospects.

"Anthropic is a once-in-a-generation company," Seth told Bloomberg this week, noting how it has grown rapidly and has strong institutional backing. "Its IPO will establish a market-clearing valuation as conditions stabilize."

Signs to watch, not reasons to flee

With many investors already running for the hills, Rees isn’t convinced the AI bubble will burst in the way skeptics expect. She thinks they should watch for stronger signs that the AI trade is maturing.

This could be "a slowdown in AI-related revenues for companies, or signs of less demand or less appetite for financing companies’ AI plans, be it through debt or through equity offerings," Rees told DW.

There are early signs that investors have less appetite for AI-related debt. Borrowing costs for AI infrastructure firms like CoreWeave and Oracle have soared recently. Even the cost of insuring Nvidia’s debt against default has risen 76% in a month, CNBC reported last week.

"They [Oracle] have been spending, some people say, like drunken sailors," Dick told DW. "They’ve compromised their balance sheet to a point where the stock’s fallen 65% from the highs."

That has not stopped Oracle, along with Meta, Microsoft and Alphabet, from continuing to issue new AI bonds. Since the end of last month, the four AI giants have announced deals worth $67 billion.

Rees said another sign could be any new regulations that make it harder to build out US data centers.

This summer, New York and Texas temporarily paused new data center approvals. Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, a Democrat who takes office in January, wants new laws to stop data centers’ heavy power and water use from pushing up household bills.

Is AI next in a long line of bubbles that burst?

In his upcoming book "AI Mania: Blather, Bluster, and the Bubble of All Bubbles," economist Gary Smith compares the AI boom with earlier frenzies around railroads, automobiles, television and the internet. He warns of a "frightful crash" when the AI bubble eventually pops.

When the dot-com bubble burst in 2000, the tech-heavy Nasdaq stock market index lost nearly 80% of its value. Yet, previous bubbles have often lasted far longer than expected, making the timing of any crash hard to predict.

Joachim Klement, head of market strategy at UK-based investment bank Panmure Liberum, believes a reckoning could happen as early as next year.

"My core conviction is that the AI bubble will either burst in 2027 or in 2028, so sometime in the next two years,” Klement told Bloomberg last month.

articles.title: Jensen Huang prima di tutto questo
articles.summary: Quella sua e di Nvidia è una storia cominciata in un ristorante popolare e arrivata dove non era arrivato nessuno
articles.preview: Quella sua e di Nvidia è una storia cominciata in un ristorante popolare e arrivata dove non era arrivato nessuno Il 26 settembre del 2023 Jensen Huang, uno degli uomini più potenti dell’industria tecnologica mondiale, era in un ristorante della catena Denny’s, un tipico diner popolare americano, nella città californiana di San Jose. Festeggiava i trent’anni di Nvidia, la più importante azienda di microchip statunitense, e il fatto che da poco aveva superato i mille miliardi di dollari di capitalizzazione.
articles.body:
Quella sua e di Nvidia è una storia cominciata in un ristorante popolare e arrivata dove non era arrivato nessuno

Il 26 settembre del 2023 Jensen Huang, uno degli uomini più potenti dell’industria tecnologica mondiale, era in un ristorante della catena Denny’s, un tipico diner popolare americano, nella città californiana di San Jose. Festeggiava i trent’anni di Nvidia, la più importante azienda di microchip statunitense, e il fatto che da poco aveva superato i mille miliardi di dollari di capitalizzazione. Era lì perché da ragazzo lavorava in un Denny’s, e proprio in quello di San Jose discusse per la prima volta di Nvidia con i due ingegneri Chris Malachowsky e Curtis Priem, con cui l’avrebbe poi fondata.

Quel ritorno da Denny’s dice molto del personaggio pubblico che Huang aveva costruito negli anni, prima che lo scandalo della sua relazione con una presunta spia cinese compromettesse irrimediabilmente la sua reputazione. Nella Silicon Valley Huang era un CEO estremamente riconoscibile, che partendo da un’infanzia difficile e un lavoro da lavapiatti era arrivato, passando attraverso varie crisi e fallimenti, a guidare l’azienda più strategica al mondo, e una delle più ricche.

Alla cerimonia indossava una giacca di pelle nera, come faceva ormai in quasi tutte le sue apparizioni pubbliche. Una volta, scherzando sull’immagine che si era costruito, si era presentato come «il tizio con la giacca di pelle che dice sempre le cose tre volte», ironizzando sulla sua tendenza a ripetere le cose importanti. Era una cosa che faceva spesso sia quando presentava i nuovi prodotti ai clienti, sia nelle frequenti riunioni interne all’azienda, in particolare quelle con i sessanta dirigenti che rispondevano direttamente a lui.

Tutta questa concentrazione di informazioni e potere aveva reso molto difficile immaginare Nvidia senza Huang, che infatti non aveva scelto un successore. Le rivelazioni sulle sue relazioni extraconiugali hanno però trasformato una vicenda privata in un problema di sicurezza nazionale e, dopo più di 33 anni alla guida dell’azienda, giovedì Huang si è dimesso ed è stato anche chiamato a testimoniare al Congresso.

Nelle sue dichiarazioni Huang si è definito orgoglioso e grato di essere un cittadino statunitense. La sua storia, d’altronde, è stata spesso descritta come un esempio di sogno americano che si realizza. Huang nacque a Taiwan nel 1963: a quel tempo l’isola era ancora sotto la legge marziale imposta dal presidente Chiang Kai-shek dopo la guerra civile con il Partito comunista cinese e stava appena cominciando la rapidissima trasformazione industriale che l’avrebbe resa una delle economie più avanzate dell’Asia. Quando aveva nove anni i genitori lo mandarono negli Stati Uniti insieme al fratello maggiore, da alcuni parenti.

Finirono tutti e due all’Oneida Baptist Institute, un collegio religioso del Kentucky rurale e che accoglieva ragazzi in situazioni difficili. Huang ha descritto quell’esperienza come una sorta di introduzione «hard knocks», «a bastonate», alla vita americana: ha raccontato che tutti gli studenti avevano delle mansioni (lui puliva i bagni del dormitorio dove dormivano circa 120 ragazzi), che molti studenti fumavano o portavano coltellini e che lui era stato bullizzato quasi tutti i giorni per il suo accento e per i suoi capelli lunghi.

Quando i genitori riuscirono a raggiungere lui e il fratello, la famiglia si trasferì in Oregon. A quindici anni Huang cominciò a lavorare in un Denny’s e a sedici si diplomò (partecipò anche alle competizioni di livello nazionale di tennistavolo). Si iscrisse alla facoltà di ingegneria elettronica della Oregon State University e lì conobbe Lori Mills, una delle poche studentesse della facoltà. Si sposarono cinque anni dopo, nel 1985, e poi ebbero due figli.

Nel frattempo nel 1984 Huang aveva iniziato a lavorare per alcune aziende di semiconduttori e lì incontrò due ingegneri, Chris Malachowsky e Curtis Priem. Loro lavoravano per un’azienda che progettava chip, e Huang per una che li produceva. Divennero amici e i due ingegneri proposero a Huang di fondare insieme una nuova azienda. Iniziarono a incontrarsi regolarmente da Denny’s perché lì si potevano bere tanti caffè e perché nessuno chiedeva loro di liberare il tavolo.

Decisero di iniziare a costruire processori per la grafica tridimensionale dei videogiochi. Inizialmente non avevano pensato a un nome per la loro azienda e quando dovettero registrarla ufficialmente cercarono qualcosa che contenesse le lettere “NV”, la sigla con cui salvavano i nomi di tutti i loro file di lavoro e che sta per next version, e cioè “prossima versione”. Scelsero così come nome “Nvidia”, dal latino invidia.

– Leggi anche: Quanto conta Jensen Huang per Nvidia

All’inizio le cose andarono molto male e Nvidia rischiò di fallire, ma riuscì a riprendersi con dei nuovi prodotti e un investimento della giapponese Sega. Nel 1999 si quotò in borsa e presentò la GeForce 256, il prodotto che contribuì a rendere popolare la sigla GPU (che sta per unità di elaborazione grafica). Come suggerisce il nome, le GPU erano state progettate per gestire le immagini dei videogiochi, ma riuscivano a svolgere moltissimi compiti contemporaneamente. Il loro potenziale insomma era enorme.

Nel 2006 Nvidia presentò CUDA, un insieme di strumenti che permetteva di usare le GPU anche per ambiti diversi dai videogiochi, con l’idea che ricercatori e sviluppatori trovassero nuovi modi di usarle. Ma fu soltanto sei anni dopo, nel 2012, che tre ricercatori mostrarono che una rete neurale, uno dei sistemi alla base delle moderne intelligenze artificiali, riusciva a ottenere risultati incredibili con CUDA e le GPU. Era la prima volta che Nvidia dimostrava di essere così efficace nel campo dell’AI, e Huang decise che ne avrebbe fatto la missione dell’azienda.

Nvidia cominciò a costruire prodotti sempre più specifici per queste applicazioni. Nel 2016 presentò DGX-1, un computer progettato appositamente per sviluppare sistemi di intelligenza artificiale, e il suo primo prototipo venne consegnato a OpenAI, l’azienda che avrebbe poi sviluppato ChatGPT. Nel 2017 realizzò Volta, una nuova generazione di processori con componenti progettati per accelerare i calcoli usati nelle reti neurali.

La domanda per i processori di Nvidia crebbe enormemente. Alle prestazioni eccezionali dei suoi chip si aggiungeva un vantaggio che i concorrenti facevano molta fatica a replicare: su CUDA e sulle GPU di Nvidia si erano accumulati anni di software, strumenti e competenze. Quando a partire dal 2022 ci fu la rapida ascesa dell’intelligenza artificiale generativa, quella di ChatGPT e Claude, Nvidia era già diventata indispensabile per lo sviluppo dei modelli più avanzati.

Intanto, sempre più governi avevano cominciato a considerare la capacità di costruire grandi sistemi di intelligenza artificiale una questione economica e strategica e avevano iniziato a fare accordi con Nvidia. Nel 2022, però, il governo statunitense decise di imporre delle restrizioni sulla vendita dei suoi chip più avanzati di Nvidia, sostenendo che potessero essere usati per scopi militari. Da quel momento sempre più decisioni commerciali di Nvidia iniziarono a passare direttamente dalle politiche di sicurezza nazionale americana, e viceversa Nvidia cominciò a influenzare le politiche pubbliche sull’AI.

Le restrizioni commerciali iniziarono però a farsi sempre più severe, e così Huang cominciò a fare pressione sull’amministrazione Biden. Insieme ad altri CEO sosteneva che limitare troppo l’accesso cinese ai chip americani avrebbe potuto ridurre i ricavi necessari alle aziende statunitensi per investire sulle nuove tecnologie, e spingere la Cina a sviluppare più rapidamente delle alternative proprie.

Huang aveva anche cominciato a promuovere quella che chiamava «sovereign AI», intelligenza artificiale sovrana, e cioè l’idea che ciascun paese dovesse sviluppare una propria AI: fece accordi con le aziende che le stavano sviluppando in molti paesi, come la saudita Humain e la Mistral francese.

La richiesta dei chip Nvidia continuava a crescere. Nell’anno fiscale 2024 Nvidia fatturò 60,9 miliardi di dollari, più del doppio dell’anno precedente. Huang ha raccontato di essersi fatto tatuare il logo di Nvidia, e di aver pianto un po’ mentre glielo facevano.

Huang era diventato anche uno dei maggiori sostenitori dei modelli di intelligenza artificiale aperti, e cioè quelli che chiunque può scaricare e adattare alle proprie esigenze. Era una strategia molto conveniente per Nvidia, perché più sono le persone che possono costruire e modificare modelli propri, più aumenta la domanda per i computer necessari ad addestrarli e farli funzionare.

Questa posizione sui modelli aperti era molto diversa da quella dell’amministrazione Biden, e molto in linea con quella di Trump. Nel suo piano nazionale sull’IA il governo trumpiano aveva dedicato un’intera sezione proprio ai modelli aperti: il rapporto sosteneva che favorissero lo sviluppo delle imprese e quindi la crescita economica statunitense. Sottolineava, inoltre, che avrebbero potuto diventare degli standard internazionali e quindi dare agli Stati Uniti anche un vantaggio geopolitico.

Anche per questo allineamento i rapporti tra Huang e Trump si erano fatti sempre più stretti: il 25 marzo Trump lo aveva nominato nel consiglio che dà indicazioni direttamente al presidente sulle politiche scientifiche e tecnologiche e a maggio lo aveva invitato personalmente ad accompagnarlo nella sua visita in Cina. Secondo il New York Times, Trump sapeva della relazione di Huang con la presunta spia cinese Alice Huang già dal 2025.

articles.body:
Nvidia

Jensen Huang, the leather-jacketed architect of the artificial intelligence boom, resigned as chief executive of Nvidia on Thursday after revelations of two extramarital affairs, including one with a woman accused of spying for China.

The scandal has wiped almost half a trillion dollars off Nvidia's market capitalisation, as it raises national security fears and leaves the AI industry in uncharted waters.

Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress, will serve as interim CEO while Nvidia's board searches for a successor, ending Huang's 33 years at the helm of the company he co-founded.

Huang, 63, also gave up his board seat. Nvidia did not give a reason for his departure.

Huang was a central figure in the boom set off by the launch of OpenAI's ChatGPT in 2022, with Nvidia’s processors, once designed for video game graphics, becoming the crucial ingredient for building AI models.

He was also a close informal adviser to President Donald Trump on AI, and had spent years lobbying against curbs on sales of advanced AI chips to China.

Nvidia shares fell as much as 13 percent following the announcement before paring losses to about four percent, wiping roughly $450 billion off the company’s value since the weekend.

Dan Ives of investment bank Yorkville Ives called it "a dark day for Nvidia and the US tech industry," but said the board had done what it needed to: "rip off the band-aid and take Nvidia into its next chapter without him."

The board named Harvey Jones, a former chief executive of chip design software firm Synopsys, as chair, and said it expected the company’s operations and product roadmap "to continue without interruption."

Interim CEO Kress joined Nvidia in 2013 after nearly 25 years at companies including Cisco and Microsoft.

Trump, who had stood by Huang throughout the scandal, said former Apple boss Tim Cook should take over.

"A Legend replaces a Legend!" Trump said on his Truth Social network.

"Tim Cook took a lot of these brilliant ideas and designs and everything else from Jobs and others, and he made it into one of the great companies of the world at a fairly short range. I think Tim Cook would be a great candidate to run Nvidia," wrote the president.

Huang remains Nvidia's largest individual shareholder, with a stake of about 3.6 percent, according to the company’s most recent filing.

For many in Silicon Valley, the departure recalls that of Steve Jobs, who was pushed out of Apple by its board in 1985 and returned 12 years later to take the company to new heights.

- Two alleged affairs -

Huang, who has been married to his wife Lori for more than 40 years, admitted on Sunday to an affair, reportedly with Alice Huang, a former senior executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed. The two are not related.

US intelligence reportedly circulated a memo this spring alleging she was an asset of China's Ministry of State Security. Beijing has rejected the allegations.

Singapore said Thursday it had barred Alice Huang, a Chinese national, from re-entering the country in February for giving investigators inaccurate information about her role at Megaspeed, though she was not investigated for espionage.

Nvidia's board opened a probe on Sunday into reporting that Huang had been the target of a "foreign intelligence effort," while saying it retained confidence in him.

When asked Thursday if Jensen should have stepped down, Trump said it depended on whether the woman was indeed a Chinese spy.

"If the woman was a spy, yes. If the woman was not a spy, perhaps it would be different," Trump said in an interview with sports commentator Stephen A. Smith.

But Trump said he was confident that Huang will "end up on his feet."

"I spoke to him yesterday. He's going through hell. What he feels most badly about is his wife and family," the president said.

On Wednesday, The New York Times reported a second affair, citing video of Huang being affectionate with Nvidia’s vice president of health care, Kimberly Powell.

- US-China tech race -

At the heart of the spy allegations is the race between the United States and China for supremacy in an industry widely seen as the next industrial revolution.

Key US lawmakers, including Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, called Thursday for answers on what the Trump administration knew about Huang's ties to a suspected Chinese intelligence asset, days before Trump travels to China for a summit.

Reports allege the Commerce Department under Secretary Howard Lutnick may have failed to act on suspicions that Megaspeed was helping reroute restricted Nvidia technology to China.

Singapore's home ministry said it had repeatedly sought information from the US Justice Department and FBI on a US server supplier during its Megaspeed probe, but "received limited information or assistance."

articles.title: Chi prenderà il posto di Jensen Huang?
